The Quiet Rise of Urban Kelp Farms

By Mara Ellison

On a converted barge moored beside the Brooklyn waterfront, a dozen volunteers spent the morning threading young kelp strands through lengths of rope, a task that looks agricultural and is, in fact, aquaculture of the most patient kind: the seaweed will grow for five months before anyone harvests a single blade.

The project is one of roughly forty small kelp farms that have appeared along the northeastern coast of the United States in the past six years. Most are run by nonprofits, universities or fishing cooperatives rather than by large companies, and almost all of them describe the same three goals: clean the water, create winter work for fishermen, and prove that a crop grown without fertilizer can pay for itself.

Kelp absorbs nitrogen and phosphorus as it grows, which is precisely what coastal waters receive too much of from septic systems, lawn runoff and sewage overflows. A single acre of the stuff can pull several tons of nitrogen out of the water in a season, though researchers caution that the effect is local and temporary once the crop is hauled ashore.

That hauling is where the economics get complicated. Fresh kelp spoils within days, so growers either dry it, freeze it, or turn it into a shelf-stable product such as seasoning, fertilizer or a feed additive for cattle that has been shown to cut methane emissions. Each of those routes needs equipment that a volunteer-run farm cannot easily afford on its own.

Some operations have responded by sharing infrastructure. A cooperative in Maine now runs a single drying facility for nine member farms, and a university lab in Connecticut lends out testing equipment in exchange for data. The arrangement keeps capital costs low, but it also means that a bad season for one farm becomes a bad season for the shared dryer, and the schedule has to be negotiated every spring.

Whether any of this survives depends less on biology than on bookkeeping. Kelp grows fast and needs no fresh water, but it also sells for modest prices, and the market for the finished products is still small. Growers say the next few seasons will decide which of the forty projects become businesses and which remain demonstrations.
